title: Networking Is the New GPU: Arista's Numbers Prove It
subtitle: A first $3 billion quarter, a full-year guide raised to $12.6 billion, and an AI target lifted again to at least $3.6 billion — Arista is becoming the tollbooth of the AI buildout.
summary: Arista Networks just posted its first $3 billion quarter — revenue up 37.7 percent, EPS up 39.7 percent — and raised its full-year outlook to roughly $12.6 billion for the third time in 2026. With deferred revenue of $6.9 billion, $9.7 billion in purchase commitments, and hyperscaler endorsements across its 1.6T portfolio, the AI Ethernet tollbooth is just getting built.

bodyHtml:
Every AI buildout has a choke point, and Arista Networks just proved which layer owns it. The company posted its first $3 billion quarter on August 4 — revenue of $3.04 billion, up 37.7 percent year over year and well above the $2.8 billion it guided to in May. Non-GAAP earnings per share of $1.02 beat the $0.89 consensus by nearly 15 percent. This is a company that told the Street it would grow, then grew harder than it promised.

That prepaid signal matters because of what it says about the AI buildout's next bottleneck. GPUs get all the headlines, but a hundred-thousand-accelerator cluster is useless if the network can't move the data between them fast enough. Every training run is a networking problem as much as a compute problem, and the market is only now figuring out who owns that layer. Arista has been quietly owning it for years — and the numbers it keeps posting make the case louder every quarter.

Walk the numbers and the consistency is almost boring, in the best way. Revenue of $3.04 billion was up 37.7 percent year over year, and non-GAAP EPS of $1.02 rose 39.7 percent — the latest in a streak of EPS beats that now stretches back more than a year. Gross margin recovered to 63.4 percent, up a full point from the prior quarter, helped by tariff refunds and a richer customer mix. Operating margin hit 49.9 percent. The result: net income of $1.3 billion, or 42.9 percent of revenue — a profit margin that looks like software, on a hardware business.

Management then did what it has done all year: it raised the bar again. Full-year 2026 revenue guidance now sits at roughly $12.6 billion, implying 40 percent growth — the third raise of the year, up from $11.5 billion in May and $10.5 billion at Analyst Day. For the third quarter, Arista guided to about $3.3 billion in revenue with EPS of $1.06 to $1.08. The AI networking target also moved again, to at least $3.6 billion for 2026, after starting the year at $3.25 billion.

The conviction behind those numbers is sitting on the balance sheet. Deferred revenue climbed to $6.9 billion — up roughly 28 percent since year-end, with customers prepaying sometimes a year or more in advance. Purchase commitments ballooned to $9.7 billion, up from $3.6 billion a year ago, as Arista locks in supply years out. Combined with $13.3 billion in cash and marketable securities and zero debt, this is a company collecting deposits on demand that's already booked.

On the product side, the moat is getting deeper. The 1.6T portfolio, anchored by the 7060XE7 Series launched in June, pushes 100 Tbps per system on Broadcom Tomahawk 6 silicon with linear pluggable optics. Meta is endorsing it for liquid-cooled next-gen training and inference. Microsoft is deploying it across Azure Maia and Fairwater datacenters. Oracle is building OCI RDMA fabrics on it. When hyperscalers name your product in their build plans, that's not a vendor relationship — that's a standard.

The customer base is the quiet revolution here. Arista now counts more than 100 Etherlink AI customers — a long way from the handful it had in 2024 — and international revenue jumped to 23 percent of the total, evidence the story is spreading beyond the usual suspects. Diversification was the biggest knock on this stock for years; it's becoming the bull case.

Now the honest risks, because there are real ones. Supply chain constraints remain a genuine 1-2 year issue — that $9.7 billion in purchase commitments is Arista managing scarcity, not splurging. Customer concentration is still a live concern, with cloud and AI giants driving a large share of revenue. And the competition is elite: NVIDIA keeps pushing into networking, and Cisco just doubled its AI infrastructure order target to $9 billion.

Here's the bottom line. The AI trade has been mostly about chips, power, and servers — but the network is the layer that connects all of them, and Arista is the tollbooth. With prepaid demand, an AI target that keeps climbing, hyperscaler endorsements, and a balance sheet that could fund a small country, the setup is about as clean as it gets. The bears will point to concentration and supply risk, and they're not wrong. But a $6.9 billion deferred revenue wall and customers prepaying for capacity a year out? That's not a cyclical story. That's infrastructure.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in ANET. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
